batchName: Late Republic: The Social War and Sulla (91-78 BCE) - Medium Batch 2
chapterName: Late Republic: The Social War and Sulla (91-78 BCE)

questions.question: Why did ancient critics condemn Sulla's generous peace with Mithridates in 85 BC?
options: They claimed it handed Athens back to Mithridates
They said he had accepted a huge personal bribe from the king
They said it abandoned Rome's ally Parthia
They called it a betrayal made so he could hurry home for revenge
They believed it broke an oath sworn to the Senate
questions.explanation: Critics saw the lenient terms as a way to free Sulla for civil war at home. He landed at Brundisium in spring 83 BC with five legions.
questions.sourceQuote: Ancient critics called it a betrayal, made so Sulla could hurry home for revenge.

questions.question: Why would packing the new citizens into a few new voting tribes limit their influence?
options: Votes from new tribes counted only half as much
Each tribe cast one vote regardless of how many members it had
New tribes were only allowed to meet outside Italy
Members of new tribes could not stand for any public office
New tribes were not permitted to vote on matters of war
questions.explanation: Romans voted in thirty-five tribes, each casting a single vote. Crowding many new citizens into a few tribes would give them few votes overall.
questions.sourceQuote: Romans voted in thirty-five voting tribes (*tribus*), and each tribe cast one vote regardless of size.

questions.question: Why did one historian call Rome's victory in the Social War "a Pyrrhic one at best"?
options: It produced both Sulla and an army willing to march on Rome
The rebel state of Italia survived the war
Mithridates used it to conquer Greece permanently
The Samnites were never actually defeated
Rome lost the loyalty of all its Latin allies
questions.explanation: The war brought large armies back onto Italian soil and taught soldiers to fight fellow Italians. That paved the way for Sulla's march on Rome.
questions.sourceQuote: One historian calls Rome's victory "a Pyrrhic one at best," since it produced both Sulla and an army willing to march on Rome.

questions.question: According to ancient writers, where did the once-penniless Sulla's fortune come from?
options: Plunder taken during the war in Numidia
Profits from writing and staging comic farces
A dowry from marrying into Marius's family
Inheritances from a stepmother and an older mistress
Bribes taken while governing Asia Minor
questions.explanation: Ancient writers credit two inheritances for Sulla's wealth. In his poor youth he had mixed with actors, musicians and dancers.
questions.sourceQuote: His later fortune, according to ancient writers, came from two inheritances: one from a loving stepmother and one from an older mistress.

questions.question: Which consequences fell on a man named in Sulla's proscriptions? (select all that apply)
options: His sons and grandsons were barred from office
His wife was sold into slavery
Anyone could kill him and claim a reward
His family was exiled to an island
His property went to the state
questions.explanation: Proscribed men could be killed by anyone for a reward, their estates were seized, and their descendants barred from office. Many were killed simply for their estates, auctioned cheaply to Sulla's friends.
questions.sourceQuote: His property went to the state, and his sons and grandsons were barred from office.

questions.question: Who joined forces to seize Rome late in 87 BC while Sulla was in Greece?
options: Cinna and the returning Marius
Drusus and the Samnite leaders
The tribune and the Senate
The Marsi and the Lucanians
Agents sent by Mithridates
questions.explanation: Cinna, consul for 87 BC, allied with Marius. They seized Rome, killed opponents and declared Sulla an outlaw; Marius died soon after.
questions.sourceQuote: Behind him, Cinna, an enemy of Sulla elected consul for that year, joined forces with the returning Marius.

questions.question: What has an influential modern historian argued since 1998 about the allies' aims?
options: They were acting as Drusus's private army in Roman politics
They were secretly paid and armed by Mithridates of Pontus
They wanted citizenship even more than ancient writers admitted
They rose to throw off Roman domination, angered by land seizures
They were mainly leading a revolt of rural slaves
questions.explanation: He argues there is little sign of Italians clamouring for citizenship before the war. Instead, land seizures drove them to seek independence.
questions.sourceQuote: Instead, he suggests, the allies were angered by Roman land seizures and rose to throw off Roman domination altogether.

questions.question: What did a tribune propose in 88 BC that Sulla opposed?
options: Granting full citizenship to all freed slaves
Abolishing the consulship for ten years
Spreading the new Italian citizens across all thirty-five tribes
Handing out more public land to the urban poor
Recalling Marius from exile in Africa
questions.explanation: The tribune wanted the new citizens distributed through all the voting tribes, increasing their power. To pass it, he struck a secret deal with Marius.
questions.sourceQuote: Then a tribune proposed spreading the new Italian citizens across all thirty-five voting tribes.

questions.question: What did Rome do for the first time because of severe manpower shortages in the Social War?
options: Conscripted boys under sixteen
Hired Greek mercenaries from the East
Enlisted freed slaves as soldiers
Recruited Gallic tribesmen as auxiliaries
Made senators serve as common soldiers
questions.explanation: Freed slaves were enlisted because manpower was so short. Rome fielded an estimated 140,000 men in fourteen legions against some 100,000 rebels.
questions.sourceQuote: Manpower was so short that freed slaves were enlisted for the first time.

questions.question: Which people, Rome's oldest allies, stayed loyal during the Social War?
options: The Latins
The Marsi
The Lucanians
The Picentes
The Samnites
questions.explanation: The Latins remained on Rome's side. Even so, Rome was so short of men that it enlisted freed slaves for the first time.
questions.sourceQuote: The Latins, Rome's oldest allies, stayed loyal.
